stimulus.text:
Andrew Jackson, Farewell Address, March 4, 1837:

“At every hazard, and by every sacrifice, this Union must be preserved.”

“If the sordid feelings of mere selfishness shall usurp the place which ought to be filled by public spirit, the legislation of Congress will soon be converted into a scramble for personal and sectional advantages.”

Background: Jackson spoke as he left the presidency after two terms that included the nullification crisis of 1832–1833, when South Carolina tried to void the federal tariff.
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from Andrew Jackson, Farewell Address, March 4, 1837, public domain, as printed by the University of Texas Core Texts collection.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Andrew Jackson, Farewell Address, March 4, 1837, public domain
stem: Jackson had crushed nullification in 1833, yet in 1837 he still warned that the Union was in danger. What does that pair of facts best show?

options.text: Defeating nullification once did not end the sectional quarrels
Jackson had changed his mind and now supported nullification
options.misconception: In 1837 he still insists the Union must be preserved, so he had not changed sides.

options.text: The tariff had been abolished entirely by 1837
options.misconception: The Compromise Tariff lowered rates step by step; tariffs were not abolished.

options.text: South Carolina had already left the Union by 1837
options.misconception: South Carolina stayed in the Union after the compromise of 1833.

rationales.A: One victory settled one crisis. The selfishness Jackson names in 1837 is the same quarrel, still alive.
rationales.B: His 1837 words repeat his 1833 stand. He still says the Union must be preserved at every hazard.
rationales.C: The Compromise Tariff of 1833 cut rates over ten years. A tariff still stood in 1837.
rationales.D: South Carolina accepted the Compromise Tariff and stayed. No state had left the Union in 1837.
rationales.general:
1. Put the two dates together. Jackson beat nullification in 1833 and still feared for the Union in 1837.
2. Ask what survived the victory. The tariff fight ended, but the habit of putting section before Union did not.
3. Name the lesson. Winning one fight does not cure the quarrel behind it.
Background: The Compromise Tariff of 1833 lowered rates gradually over ten years and ended the crisis.
Remember: when a danger outlives its first defeat, look for the quarrel underneath it.
